structure.title: Introduction
structure.text:
LITHIUM ION CONDUCTORS IN THE SYSTEM AB(IV)2(P04) 3 (B = Ti, Zr AND Hf)

M.A. SUBRAMANIAN, Rajeevi SUBRAMANIAN and A. CLEARFIELD

Department of Chemistry, Texas A & M University, College Station, Texas, 77843, U.S.A.

Lithium ion conductors based on LiB2(P04) 3 (B = Ti, Zr and Hf) type structures have been synthesized by suitable substitution at the B site. Solid solutions of the type LiZr2-xTix(P04)3, Li1+xScxTi2\_x(P04) 3 and Li1+xlnxHf2\_x(P04) 3 are found to exist for various values of x and their lithium conductivities are determined. The results are discussed in terms of the number of conductors, bottleneck size and stoichiometry.

structure.title: Abstract / Introduction
structure.text:
Lithium ion conductors are especially attractive for a number of reasons. Lithium is relatively inexpensive, has an extremely high reduction potential (Ere d = -3.024V) and is light in weight. Thus, lithium based batteries would have a high open circuit voltage and exhibit high energy density. I Therefore, a good lithium conductor, with the requisite ceramic properties, has been a goal of our research for a number of years. In this paper we concern ourselves with lithium ion conductors, based upon the LiM(IV)2(P04) 3 framework. These compounds are related to the NASICON solid solutions of composition Na1+xZr2SixP3\_xOl2 • The end member, NaZr2(P04) 3, has a low conductivity, but as x increases so does the conductivity reaching a maximum for 1.8 ~ x ~ 2.3. 2 A silicate containing lithium ion series could not be prepared, but Li3Zr2Si2P012 was obtained from the corresponding sodium analogue by ion exchange. 2

Its conductivity is three orders of magnitude lower than the conductivity of its sodium ion counterpart. A search by Hong for additional framework structures which would satisfy the criteria 3 for fast Li + conduction led to the discovery of Lii4Zn(Ge04) 4. However, the M(IV) 2 (PO 4)3 framework al lows a large number of substitutions to be made with retention of

basic structure and properties. 5-9 Thus, it was felt that fast lithium ion conductors could be prepared by a combination of nonstoichiometry and proper framework substitutions. This paper details the results of our initial efforts. I0

structure.title: 2.1 Synthetic Procedure
structure.text:
Li3PO 4, TiO 2 and ZrO 2 (hafnium free) were spec. pure grade from Johnson Matthey, Inc. ZrP 0 and TiP 0 were prepared by heating 2 7 2 7 ii m-zirconium phosphate and m-titanium phosphate 12 respectively, at IO00°C for 4 hr. The phosphates in turn were prepared by standard procedures. 11'12 The pyrophosphates were dissolved in dilute HF, analyzed by ICP and found to contain less than lOOppm of impurities. Sc203, In203 and HfO 2 from Aldrich Chemical Co. were 99.99% pure.

The reagents (ZrO 2, TiO 2, Li3PO 4 and Sc203) were dried in an oven at 300°C for 4- 8 hr just prior to use and stored in a desiccator. Exact mole ratios of the ingredients were weighed out and ground together in an agate mortar until thoroughly blended. The entire solid was then transferred to a platinum tube (4mm O.D.) and sealed by cold pressing. The tube was heated at 800°C for 6 hr and then for 20 hr in the temperature range 1000-1100°C.

Exact mole ratios of the ingredients were weighed out and ground together in an agate mortar until thoroughly blended. The entire solid was then transferred to a platinum tube (4mm O.D.) and sealed by cold pressing. The tube was heated at 800°C for 6 hr and then for 20 hr in the temperature range 1000-1100°C.

structure.title: 2.2 Instrumental Procedures
structure.text:
Powder patterns were recorded with a Siefert-Scintag automated powder diffractometer (PAD-II) using CuK~ radiation. Patterns were step scanned (0.03°28/5 sec) and peaks located after data transfer to a larger computer. Peak positions were corrected by means of an internal calibrant (NBS-SRM #640 - Si powder) and cell parameters were found by indexing programs VISIND and TREOR 13. Cell parameters were then least squared refined by program LSUCRE 13.

lonic conductivity measurements were performed on the samples in the form of sintered pellets by the complex impedance method. 14 The pellets (8mm dia. and 2-3mm thick) were made at room temperature in an evacuative die at i0 tons/sq, inch and the pellets were sintered at I150-1200°C for 24 hrs in a closed platinum crucible. These pressed and sintered pellets were polished with 400 grade emery paper and the faces were coated with conductive platinum paint (Englehard 6042) and heated at 600°C to

evaporate the solvent. For conductivity measurements the pellets were sandwiched between two platinum plates which were spring loaded to ensure good electrolyte/electrode contact. Impedance measurements were performed in the frequency region 5 Hz to 13 MHz using an HP 4192A impedance analyzer, and when required, to 108 MHz with an HP 4815 unit. Further details are given in ref. 15.

The value given in the Table for LiZr2(P04) 3 is for the triclinic (or possibly monoclinic) phase. It is seen that LiTi2(P04) 3 exhibits a conductivity about two orders of magnitude greater than the zirconium compound. However, there is not a smooth transition from one end member to the other. In the region of high disorder the powders were difficult to sinter and consequently the compacts were of lower density. Thus, these values are subject to greater error. If we disregard the value for LiZrTi(P04) 3, the conductivity appears to increase with a decrease in cell parameters until a maximum in the conductivity is achieved for LiZro.2TiI.8(P04) 3 3.2 Sc 3+ Substitution in LiTi2P3012 In order to improve the conductivity, Sc 3+ was added as a partial replacement for Ti 4+ according to the formula LiL+xScxTi2\_x(P04) 3. Unit cell data for compositions with values of x between 0 and 1 are shown in Table 2 and plotted in Figure 2. Since Sc 3+ is slightly larger than Ti 4+ the effect of the substitution is to increase the cell parameters in a linear fashion. However, when x = 0.5 the powder lines split in a manner indicative of formation of a lattice of lower symmetry, probably monoclinic. However, we could "not index the pattern. At a value of x = 1.0, further splitting of the lines occurs and the crystal system could not be identified. Conductivity data for the scandium containing solids are shown in Table 3. A dramatic increase in the magnitude of the conductivity appears with respect to the mixed titaniumzirconium composition. The differences in cell volumes for the scandium containing solids versus the Ti-Zr mixed compositions are very minor. Thus, the bulk of the conductivity change must result from the increase in Li + content. It is further seen that the conductivity passes through a maximum at x = 0.3. This may represent the point at which the cavities become very large relative to the size of the lithium ion resulting in stronger binding of the cation to the lattice oxygens. Arrhenius plots of log ~ versus the reciprocal of the absolute temperature are shown in Figure 3. It is seen that the curves divide into two straight lines. The slopes below IO0°C give values of E = 0.I eV for x = 0.2 a and 0.3, respectively. At the higher temperature range the activation energies are about 4 times higher. The X-ray pattern resembles that for LiI.5SCo.5TiI.5(P04) 3 with the reflection shifted slightly to a lower angle indicative of larger cell parameters. At the high Zr end of the series, LiI.2SCo.2Zrl.6Tio.2(P04) 3, the powder pattern could be indexed with a monoclinic cell. Conductivity data for two of the Sc-Ti-Zr compositions is shown in Table 3 and Figure 4. 3.3 In 3+ Substitution in LiHf2(P04) 3 Taylor et al. 6 have reported that LiHf2(P04) 3 crystallizes with a rhombohedral structure similar to NaZr2(P04) 3. We attempted to improve the conductivity of LiHf2(P04) 3 by substituting Hf with a slightly larger cation, In 3+. Cell parameters for Lit+xlnxHf2\_x(P04) 3 compositions are given in Table 4. In this case, ~c solid solutions exist up to x = 3. For higher values of x, the X-ray patterns were complex due to the lowering of symmetry. Conductivity data for the above compositions are also given in Table 4 and Figure 5. As observed by Taylor et al., the conductivity of LiHf2(P04) 3 is higher than that of the corresponding Zr compound (Table 1). Substitution of Hf by In 3+ increased the Li ion conductivity slightly within the R-3c solid solutions.

The crystal structure of triphosphates of the type AIM21v(P04) 3 consists of a three dimensional network of phosphate tetrahedra and MO 6 octahedra sharing corners. 2'3'8 This arrangement forms Zr2(P04) ~ groups and each group is linked to others by PO 4 tetrahedra. Adjacent layers are shifted by 1/2 along the C axis. r The new cavities (type II) which arise from this positioning of the layers have 8-10 oxygen atoms which coordinate Na + compared to six in a trigonal prism arrangement in the type I cavities which coordinate Na +. In the NASICON solid solution, Nal+xZr2SixP3\_xOl2, sodium ions fill the type II cavities as their numbers increase with increasing silicon content. At the same time, the passageways connecting the cavities increase in size allowing freer movement of sodium ions with consequent rise in conductivity. In contrast, the very low conductivity of NaZr2(P04) 3 results from the narrowness of the passageways leading from type I to type II cavities which severely restrict Na + mobility. Another factor working against high mobility of the conducting ions is their tight binding to the framework oxygens. This factor must become very important in the Li + compounds as discussed below.

A very large increase in conductivity takes place upon substitution of Ti 4+ for Zr 4+ in the framework and a further increase takes place when relatively small amounts of Sc 3+ are substituted for Ti 4+ in LiTi2(P04) 3. A maximum in the conductivity was achieved for Lil.3SCo.3Ti].7P3012 and shows that there is a critical interplay of several factors respon-

sible for increased conductivity. We may enumerate these in keeping with previous deductions 3 as (1) The size of the cavities in which the Li + resides; (2) The size of the bottlenecks to diffusion~ (3) The strength of the Li-lattice oxygen bonds. Of course, increasing the number of conductors while leaving sufficient cavities empty must also be considered. Some of these factors are clearly illustrated by the present study. Most striking is the increase in conduc-

tivity when the smaller titanium ion is substituted for Zr 4+. This change undoubtedly decreases the size of the cavities as evidenced by the large decrease in cell parameters (~0.3A in both a and c). The closer proximity of Li + to Ti 4+ would result in a greater repulsion from the Ti 4+ ions surrounding the cavity and tend to produce weaker Li-O bonds. However, the optimum in conductivity was achieved for LiZro.2Til.8P3012 where the cell parameters are slightly larger, which may be connected with slight changes in bottleneck size also.

During the course of this work we became aware of a similar study 7 in which In3+substi tutions for Ti 4+ were carried out. In this case the maximum was achieved at 0.4 mole In. The ionic radii of In 3+ and Sc 3+ are almost identical but this difference in composition may be reflecting some small differences in electron configuration of the two ions.

The conductivity of pure LiHf2(P04) 3 is two orders of magnitude larger than that of LiZr2(P04) 3 in accordance with results obtained by Taylor et al. 6 However, increase in the

number of Li conductors by replacement of Hf by In did not result in a drastic increase in Li + ion conductivity. If one compares the unit cell and conductivity data for LiI.3SCo.3Til.7(P04) 3 with Li[.31no.3Hf1.7(P04) 3 the former has a lower unit cell volume and higher conductivity (Tables 2, 3 and 4). This indicates that the bottleneck size of the conducting path plays an important role among Li ion conductors based on the LiM2(P04) 3 type structure.

From the results reported here it would appear that the course to follow to achieve even higher Li + conductivity is proper substitution into the LiTi2P30]2 lattice so as to increase the Li + content while simultaneously adjusting cavity and bottleneck size to allow free movement of the ions. In this connection we have achieved a composition of **Lil.6Gao.6Til.4(P04)3** with R3c structure. Con-Juctivity measurements are in progress

nodes.title: Sodium Ion Mobility and Limiting Factors
nodes.text: In the NASICON solid solution, Nal+xZr2SixP3\_xOl2, sodium ions fill the type II cavities as their numbers increase with increasing silicon content. At the same time, the passageways connecting the cavities increase in size allowing freer movement of sodium ions with consequent rise in conductivity. In contrast, the very low conductivity of NaZr2(P04) 3 results from the narrowness of the passageways leading from type I to type II cavities which severely restrict Na + mobility. Another factor working against high mobility of the conducting ions is their tight binding to the framework oxygens. This factor must become very important in the Li + compounds as discussed below.

nodes.title: Comparative Analysis of Other Substitutions
nodes.text:
During the course of this work we became aware of a similar study 7 in which In3+substi tutions for Ti 4+ were carried out. In this case the maximum was achieved at 0.4 mole In. The ionic radii of In 3+ and Sc 3+ are almost identical but this difference in composition may be reflecting some small differences in electron configuration of the two ions. The conductivity of pure LiHf2(P04) 3 is two orders of magnitude larger than that of LiZr2(P04) 3 in accordance with results obtained by Taylor et al. 6 However, increase in the

number of Li conductors by replacement of Hf by In did not result in a drastic increase in Li + ion conductivity. If one compares the unit cell and conductivity data for LiI.3SCo.3Til.7(P04) 3 with Li[.31no.3Hf1.7(P04) 3 the former has a lower unit cell volume and higher conductivity (Tables 2, 3 and 4). This indicates that the bottleneck size of the conducting path plays an important role among Li ion conductors based on the LiM2(P04) 3 type structure.
